text: You have Parquet in S3 and a table in the catalog. Before you pull anything into pandas, ask whether SQL can answer the question, or shrink the data first. Amazon Athena runs SQL directly on catalog tables, with no cluster to start. Here we use it the way a data scientist does.

Athena has three jobs in a data science workflow. Explore and aggregate with SQL, so only small results travel to your notebook. Sample the data in a way you can repeat. And build a training table with a single statement. Since we have no Athena to call, I ran the SQL in SQLite as a stand-in. Details differ, so always retest on Athena.

Does churn differ by plan? This query grouped fifty thousand synthetic customers. Basic churned at nineteen percent, plus at eighteen point six, pro at nineteen point three. Plan alone barely moves churn, and only three small rows came back to the notebook.

For sampling, Athena supports TABLESAMPLE BERNOULLI, but it is random, so two runs give different rows. For repeatable experiments, filter on a key instead, such as customer ID modulo ten. You keep the same customers every time, just like fixing a random seed.

CREATE TABLE AS SELECT, or CTAS, builds a table from a query. In Athena you set the format to Parquet and choose an S3 location. Two rules from the docs: the location must be empty, since Athena never deletes data, and a workgroup that enforces a results location will make this fail. This is illustrative, not run here.

From Python, the AWS SDK for pandas reads an Athena query straight into a DataFrame. With plain boto3, you start the query, poll its status, then fetch results. This snippet is illustrative and needs an AWS account.
Athena bills by data scanned, so select only the columns you need and store training tables as Parquet. Next, Redshift for analytics.
